paper.title: Image Tokenizers Should Be Trained Between Images
paper.abstract:
Abstract Latent diffusion models generate images as codes of an image tokenizer, whose decoder turns them into the pixel image.
Recent tokenizers improve how well these codes reconstruct an image and how easily a generator learns them.
Yet a generator does not reproduce the codes of training images, and when a generated code lands outside what the decoder expects, the decoded image contains imperfections.
Current methods make the decoder more robust to generated codes by adding noise during training.
However, generated codes lie between the training codes and resemble their mixture more than one of them plus noise.
To improve generated images, decoders should therefore be trained on codes in the space between training samples.
We propose InterpTok , which fine-tunes MAETok to decode mixtures of image codes into natural images.
Since no target image exists between two training samples, a discriminator judges whether each decoded mixture looks as natural as its two sources.
A mixing ratio loss requires the decoded mixture to keep the mixing ratio of the two codes.
Together, they prevent collapse to a trivial solution and yield a sharp and natural composition of both images.
InterpTok keeps MAETok’s reconstruction quality and improves interpolation quality more than threefold, the best of all tokenizers in a recent benchmark.
Beyond interpolation, InterpTok improves the generation FID of a matched diffusion transformer from 11.61 to 8.48 without guidance, and even reaches 8.11 at an eighth of the sampling steps, where the generator on MAETok’s codes worsens.
The generator trained on our tokenizer also reaches the final result of the one trained on MAETok at half the training steps.
Our findings show that the space between image codes can and should be explicitly supervised rather than ignored.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Modern image generation largely relies on diffusion and flow matching models ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Ma et al., 2024 ) . These models generate images through many refinement steps, so most operate in a compact latent space to make each step more efficient ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) . In this space, each image is represented by a compact code created by an image tokenizer. The tokenizer’s encoder turns images into codes, and its decoder turns codes back into images. The generator learns to produce these codes and therefore depends on the space created by the tokenizer. Improving image generation therefore starts with asking what makes this latent space useful for a generator. Most tokenizer methods focus on the codes of the training images and make them easier for a generator to learn ( Chen et al., 2025a ; Yao et al., 2025 ; Fan et al., 2026 ) . Standard tokenizer training, however, supervises one code at a time by reconstructing its image. It tells the decoder what to produce at the codes of the training images, but does not supervise the codes between them. As Fig. 1 illustrates, a decoder can reconstruct images A and B well and still turn a mixture of their codes into a blurry superposition. Reconstruction can therefore give us good endpoints while leaving the path between them undefined. This gap matters because a generator does not perfectly reproduce training samples but creates codes the decoder never saw. Recent work shows that generated codes lie near the lines between neighboring training codes. It also shows that the quality of images decoded on these lines predicts generation quality better than reconstruction quality does ( Xu et al., 2026 ) . The decoder must therefore work beyond the exact codes it was trained to reconstruct. Existing tokenizer and decoder training schemes add noise to training codes and make their local neighborhoods more robust ( Yang et al., 2026b ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) . They improve the visual quality of images decoded around each image code. While this improves generation, it does not target the space between training codes, where generative denoising models tend to place their codes. In this work, we argue that image tokenizers should be trained between images. We propose InterpTok, which mixes the codes of two training images at a known ratio and decodes the result. Each pair gives us an entire line of training inputs, even though no target image exists along that line. To prevent trivial solutions such as copying one source, we set two requirements the decoded mixtures must fulfill. The decoded mixture must look like a natural image, and it must remain tied to its position between the two sources. Our first component, the interpolation objective , addresses both. An interpolation discriminator compares the decoded mixture with one source at a time in the features of a frozen pretrained network and pushes it away from blurry overlays ( Caron et al., 2021 ; Sauer et al., 2021 ) . A mixing ratio loss prevents the decoder from choosing either source and keeps the result at the mixing ratio, in pixels and in the features of a frozen vision model ( Siméoni et al., 2026 ) . Together, they enforce natural-looking images that are true compositions of both sources at the right ratio, allowing supervision without target images. Interpolation and reconstruction alone do not guarantee a latent space that a generator can learn easily. In our ablations, the interpolation objective improves the visual fidelity and sharpness of images between codes, but leaving out losses that structure the latent space makes the codes harder for the generator to learn. We therefore introduce a second component, regularization losses . They align the codes with the features of the same vision model, so that images with similar content receive similar codes ( Yao et al., 2025 ) . MAETok structures its codes too, through auxiliary decoders that predict pretrained features of masked image parts, and our regularization losses replace them. InterpTok combines the interpolation objective and the regularization losses with the original reconstruction objective of MAETok ( Chen et al., 2025a ) . Our contributions can be summarized as follows: • Training Between Images: We propose a training principle for latent image tokenizers that supervises the space between image codes. An interpolation discriminator and a mixing ratio loss make the decoded mixture of two codes a natural image at the right ratio. • InterpTok: Trained end to end with the interpolation objective and our regularization losses, InterpTok improves interpolation quality more than threefold and generation quality by more than a quarter and lets its generator train and sample faster, while keeping the reconstruction quality of MAETok. • Fast Decoder Fine-Tuning: For MAETok, whose latent space is already structured, fine-tuning only the decoder with our objective is a cheap way to improve the generators already trained on it, without retraining them.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Image tokenizers. The objective of image tokenizers is to compress images into a compact latent space and to decode the codes back to images. A generative model can then be trained in this compressed space, improving efficiency and performance ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) . Early tokenizers were plain autoencoders trained to reconstruct their input ( Hinton & Salakhutdinov, 2006 ) , which leaves the shape of their latent space unconstrained. Variational autoencoders add a penalty that keeps the code distribution close to a Gaussian, which makes the latent space easier for a generator to learn ( Kingma & Welling, 2014 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ) . Compression loses information, so the optimum of a pure pixel loss is an average of the possible images, which blurs the reconstructions. VQ-GAN therefore adds a discriminator that judges whether reconstructed images look natural ( Esser et al., 2021 ) . All of them train the decoder on the codes of single images, and none trains it between two images. More recent work shapes the latent space itself instead of optimizing reconstruction alone, with 1D codes whose tokens are not tied to patches in the image ( Yu et al., 2024 ) and with codes aligned to the features of pretrained vision models ( Yao et al., 2025 ) . MAETok ( Chen et al., 2025a ) showed that a diffusion model learns the codes more easily when they form fewer and more separated clusters, and reached this structure with a plain autoencoder trained by masked modeling, where auxiliary decoders predict features of the hidden image patches from the codes. Because masking degrades reconstruction, MAETok then freezes the encoder and fine-tunes only the pixel decoder for a few epochs, which improves fine detail. Behavior of generative denoising models. Generative denoising models do not simply recreate the image codes they saw during training. This can lead to generated codes that deviate from the codes the decoder was optimized for. These out-of-distribution codes are then decoded to images with blur or artifacts. Recent work therefore trains the decoder on codes other than the clean training codes, by transforming the code ( Kouzelis et al., 2025 ) , mixing it with noise ( Yang et al., 2026b ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) or post-training on the samples of a trained generator ( Qiu et al., 2025 ) . However, Aithal et al. (2024) showed that a diffusion model interpolates between nearby modes of its training data and produces samples that exist nowhere in it, which they call mode interpolation. Xu et al. (2026) carried this to tokenizer codes, where the optimal denoiser outputs a weighted average of the training codes ( Karras et al., 2022 ) . They show empirically that the quality of decoded mixtures of image codes (iFID) predicts the generation quality (gFID) far better than reconstruction quality (rFID), which is uncorrelated with it or even negatively correlated. Generated codes therefore resemble mixtures of image codes. Supervising between images. Training an autoencoder on interpolation goes back to representation learning, where a realistic interpolation was taken as a sign that the autoencoder had captured the structure of its data instead of memorizing it ( Berthelot et al., 2019 ) . ACAI trains the autoencoder so that its decoded mixtures fool a critic that regresses the mixing coefficient ( Berthelot et al., 2019 ) , AMR ( Beckham et al., 2019 ) and Oring et al. (2021) train it against a discriminator between real and mixed images, and GAIA against an autoencoder that is trained to reconstruct real images but not mixtures ( Sainburg et al., 2018 ) . ACAI and AMR report smoother interpolations of small images, and codes that are more useful for classification. Recently, CompTok ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) argued that a generator learns a token space more easily when the images decoded along the line between the codes of two nearby images stay realistic, and measured this as mode connectivity. To raise it, CompTok trains on codes formed by swapping token subsets between two images under an adversarial realism term, but a swap composes real token values, whereas a generator produces values between two real ones ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , and CompTok does not train on the line it measures. The gap between swapped and generated values arises only for continuous tokens, as in MAETok and CompTok, since a generator of discrete tokens only selects real codebook entries. Complementary to these methods, InterpTok carries the adversarial interpolation objective to a tokenizer for latent diffusion, trains on the line that CompTok measures, and holds the decoded mixture at the mixing ratio with a mixing ratio loss.

sections.heading: 3.1 Background
sections.text: Latent diffusion. Latent diffusion models generate images in the compact latent space of an image tokenizer instead of in pixel space, since training generative models on pixels is computationally expensive ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) . The tokenizer consists of an encoder E E and a decoder D D . The encoder maps an image A A to its code a = E ⁡ ( A ) a=E(A) , which is much smaller than the image itself. The decoder maps a code back to an image. Both are trained together, so that the decoded image D ⁡ ( E ⁡ ( A ) ) D(E(A)) is close to the original image A A . A diffusion generator is then trained separately to denoise noisy image codes. To generate an image, the generator starts from pure noise and iteratively refines it into a code, which D D then decodes into the pixel image ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Ma et al., 2024 ) . Diffusion generators tend to generate codes that lie between the codes of training images ( Aithal et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . The decoder of the tokenizer, however, is trained only on the codes that the encoder produces for training images, leaving the codes between them unsupervised. MAETok. We build on MAETok ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , which shows that a diffusion model learns codes more easily when a Gaussian mixture model fits them with fewer modes. MAETok obtains such codes with a plain autoencoder, without the penalty of a variational autoencoder. Its code consists of 128 vectors, called tokens. MAETok is trained in two stages. In the first stage, a large part of every image is masked before it enters the encoder. Small auxiliary decoders then predict, from the code, the features that pretrained vision models extract from the masked parts, extending masked autoencoders ( He et al., 2022 ) from pixels to features. Masking forces the encoder to infer the hidden parts of an image from the visible ones, which leads to such codes. However, a decoder trained on the codes of partly masked images reconstructs fewer details. To address this, the second stage freezes the encoder and fine-tunes only the decoder on the codes of complete images, which recovers the lost details. We choose MAETok for three reasons. First, we want to show that our method is not limited to the decoder, and therefore choose among tokenizers that train their own encoder. Among those in the benchmark of Xu et al. (2026) that do not start from a pretrained vision model, MAETok has the highest interpolation quality. We attribute this to its masked training, where the decoder is trained to reconstruct the complete image from the code of a partly masked image. Second, its codes are continuous. In a quantized tokenizer, every token is an index into a codebook, and there is no code between two indices. Third, MAETok is a 1D tokenizer ( Yu et al., 2024 ) , whose tokens are not tied to locations in the image, while every token of a 2D tokenizer belongs to one patch. We want mixtures that interpolate between whole images, not between the patches at each location. Reconstruction objective. MAETok trains with the standard tokenizer losses ( Esser et al., 2021 ) , a pixel loss, a perceptual loss ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) and an adversarial loss. The pixel loss and the perceptual loss compare the decoded image with the original image, in pixels and in the features of a pretrained network. The adversarial loss trains the tokenizer against a discriminator that distinguishes real images from reconstructions. It enforces sharp images, whereas the optimum of a pure pixel loss is a slightly blurred image. Unlike the other two losses, it needs no target image, since the discriminator judges each image on its own. We denote these losses together as the reconstruction objective ℒ rec \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}} and their discriminator as the reconstruction discriminator.

At α = 0 \alpha=0 and α = 1 \alpha=1 the mixture is the code of a source, and in between it moves along the line from a a to b b . Fig. 1 shows what MAETok’s decoder produces on this line. Toward the middle, the decoded image superimposes both sources and is blurrier than either reconstruction. Xu et al. (2026) show that the quality of the images decoded between neighboring training codes predicts generation quality better than reconstruction quality does. Recent methods add noise to the codes during decoder training ( Yang et al., 2026b ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) , which makes the decoder more robust around each training code but does not target the space between codes. A straightforward alternative is to supervise random codes, so that every code decodes to a realistic image. However, since real images have few intrinsic dimensions ( Pope et al., 2021 ) , their codes occupy only a small part of the latent space, and random codes mostly lie far outside the training distribution. Decoding a meaningful image from an arbitrary code is far more ambiguous than decoding one between two image codes. A mixture has no target image either, but it comes with two sources and a ratio, and InterpTok uses them in place of a target image. Decodability and learnability. Two properties of a tokenizer matter for the quality of the output of a diffusion generator. We call the visual fidelity and sharpness of the images that the decoder produces from generated codes its decodability. We call how easily a conditioned generator can learn the codes of training images and tell them apart by their condition, such as their class label, the learnability of the tokenizer. This is easier when the latent space is structured such that the class of an image can be derived from where its code lies, as MAETok finds. Decodability is thus mainly a property of the decoder, and learnability of the encoder. InterpTok targets decodability with the interpolation objective of Sec. 3.3 and learnability with the regularization losses of Sec. 3.4 .

sections.heading: 3.3 Interpolation Objective
sections.text: The interpolation objective trains the tokenizer on decoded mixtures and targets decodability. It consists of an interpolation discriminator and two mixing ratio losses. Interpolation discriminator. A mixture has no target image, and we therefore supervise the decoded mixture with a discriminator. Adversarial interpolation was introduced for representation learning with small autoencoders. ACAI ( Berthelot et al., 2019 ) trains a critic to recover the mixing ratio from the decoded mixture and the autoencoder to hide it, and AMR ( Beckham et al., 2019 ) trains a discriminator that tells real images from decoded mixtures, both on small images such as MNIST, SVHN and CIFAR-10. Their critics judge the mixture alone, so any realistic image passes, whether or not it relates to the two sources, and neither keeps the mixture at the mixing ratio. Our interpolation discriminator judges the decoded mixture beside one of its sources and is trained to identify which of the two is the real image. We use it to train a tokenizer for latent diffusion on ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) at 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution. For an image X X and a second image Y Y , the features of X X in a frozen DINO network ( Caron et al., 2021 ) attend to those of Y Y through trained cross-attention layers, so that every part of X X is compared with Y Y . We call this the source conditioning of the discriminator. A trained head maps the result to the score s ⁡ ( X ∣ Y ) s(X\mid Y) , which is higher for images that look more like real images. Each decoded mixture is compared with both of its sources in turn. sections.heading: 3.4 Regularization Losses
sections.text: The interpolation objective targets decodability but not learnability. We therefore add regularization losses to structure the latent space semantically. The frozen DINOv3 model, pretrained on large image collections, describes each image by a feature vector. Alignment losses make the codes carry the semantic information of these features. VA-VAE ( Yao et al., 2025 ) aligns the code of a tokenizer with the patch features of such a model, DINOv2 ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) , at every image position and requires the similarities between the positions of a code to match those between the features. REPA ( Yu et al., 2025 ) requires the features to be predictable by a small network from the hidden states of a diffusion generator, and GigaTok ( Xiong et al., 2025 ) from the activations inside the decoder of a tokenizer. InterpTok uses three alignment losses in this spirit, which require the similarities between the codes of different images to match those between their feature vectors, the feature vector to be predictable from the code, and the features of each image patch to be predictable from the activations inside the decoder. As a result, images with more similar visual and semantic features receive more similar codes, which these works find easier for a generator to learn. MAETok ties its codes to pretrained features as well, through auxiliary decoders that predict the features of the masked image parts, and InterpTok replaces these auxiliary decoders with the three alignment losses. The representation Fréchet loss ( Yang et al., 2026a ) was introduced for post-training generators, and to our knowledge it has not been used to train a tokenizer before. It compares the distribution of the decoded images with that of the training images in the features of three frozen image encoders, SigLIP2 ( Tschannen et al., 2025 ) , Inception-v3 ( Szegedy et al., 2016 ) and MAE ( He et al., 2022 ) , and minimizes the Fréchet distance between the two. The alignment losses act on single images and the representation Fréchet loss on a subsample of the decoded images, mixtures included, and together they form ℒ reg \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}} .

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate InterpTok on reconstruction, interpolation, generation and learnability, compare it with MAETok and with the tokenizers benchmarked by Xu et al. (2026) , and ablate its components. Our experiments validate three claims. First, a modern tokenizer can be trained between images together with current regularization losses. InterpTok improves interpolation quality, generation quality and learnability while keeping reconstruction quality. Second, the regularization losses alone do not improve generation, and trained with them but without interpolation, the tokenizer has the worst gFID of all variants. Third, a conditioned generator needs both learnability, a property of the encoder, and decodability, a property of the decoder. Most of the InterpTok generation gain compared to MAETok comes from the decoder.

sections.heading: 4.1 Setup
sections.text: Implementation details. We start from the released weights of MAETok and train its encoder and decoder together on ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) at 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution. The interpolation objective replaces MAETok’s masking as a self-supervised objective. We evaluate on ImageNet and MS-COCO ( Lin et al., 2014 ) . For generation, we train a SiT-B ( Ma et al., 2024 ) conditioned on class labels with the same setting on the codes of each tokenizer. We also decode the generated codes of the SiT-XL released with MAETok ( Chen et al., 2025a ) with our decoder trained on MAETok’s frozen encoder. We sample every generator without classifier-free guidance ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) , whose strength would have to be tuned for each tokenizer. More details are provided in App. D . For reconstruction, we compare each decoded image with its original, using the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) for pixel accuracy, the Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) ( Wang et al., 2004 ) for structural preservation and the Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) for perceptual alignment. Decoded mixtures have no original to compare with. The Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) , the standard metric for the quality of generated images, needs none, since it compares the distribution of a model’s images with that of images of the dataset. Following Xu et al. (2026) , we therefore measure decoded mixtures with the interpolated FID (iFID). iFID decodes the midpoint of a spherical path between each validation code and one of its nearest training codes and computes the FID of these images. It thus serves as our measure of decodability. We also report the FID of tokenizer reconstructions (rFID) and of generated images (gFID). We measure gFID at the usual 250 sampling steps and at fewer, since fewer steps make sampling cheaper. For learnability, we conduct linear probing as MAETok does, training a linear classifier to predict the class of an image from its code, and report its accuracy. ImageNet labels every image with a class, and the generator is conditioned on this class label. We also report how often a code lies closest to the average code of its own class rather than to the average code of a different class.

sections.heading: 4.2 Main Results
sections.text: Interpolation. InterpTok sets the best interpolation quality in the comparison. In Table 1 , it reduces the iFID of MAETok more than threefold, from 14.42 to 4.30, lower than that of every tokenizer in the comparison released by Xu et al. (2026) . On random MS-COCO pairs, the FID of its decoded midpoints is six times lower than MAETok’s, as App. B.5 shows. This demonstrates that decoding between codes can be learned, and App. A shows decoded paths for thirteen image pairs. The next best, RAE ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) , whose code consists of the features of the pretrained network DINOv2, reaches 1.8 times our iFID. RAE and l-DeTok ( Yang et al., 2026b ) train their decoders on noisy codes, indicating that robustness to noise improves interpolation quality less than training between codes, as the decoder with noise augmentation of Table 3 confirms. Between the codes. Fig. 3 a shows the FID of the images that MAETok and InterpTok decode from a code to its midpoint with one of its nearest training codes. At the code, both reach about the same FID. At the midpoint, MAETok’s FID is 25 times its FID at the code, and InterpTok’s only 7 times. Their decoders thus differ most between the codes, where reconstruction metrics are not computed. Fig. 3 b shows that InterpTok reaches most of its gain at the midpoint within the first 13,000 fine-tuning steps. Figure 3: FID between two codes. (a) From a code to its midpoint with one of its nearest training codes, on a logarithmic axis. (b) The iFID of InterpTok over its fine-tuning steps. Generation. InterpTok makes generation better, cheaper to sample and faster to train. In Table 2 , replacing MAETok with InterpTok reduces the gFID of the generator from 11.61 to 8.48, in line with Xu et al. (2026) , who find that iFID predicts gFID. With an eighth of the sampling steps, and thus an eighth of the sampling cost, InterpTok’s generator reaches an even lower gFID, while the gFID of the generator on MAETok’s codes rises with every reduction of the steps. InterpTok’s generator also reaches the final gFID of MAETok’s generator after only half of the training steps. App. B.1 shows the gFID over the generator’s training, and Fig. 19 shows generated samples. Reconstruction. Training between images does not cost reconstruction quality. In Table 11 , the rFID of InterpTok on ImageNet stays within three percent of MAETok’s, and its PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS improve on both ImageNet and MS-COCO, while its rFID on MS-COCO is higher. In Table 3 , a linear classifier predicts the class from InterpTok’s codes more accurately, and App. B.9 shows that 73 percent of InterpTok’s codes lie closest to the average code of their own class, against 55 percent of MAETok’s. The class of an image can thus be derived from its code more reliably, and a model conditioned on class labels can learn more easily which codes belong to which class. Trained with interpolation but without the regularization losses, the tokenizer improves interpolation quality nearly as much as InterpTok, but a linear classifier predicts the class from its codes less accurately than from MAETok’s. Trained with the regularization losses but without interpolation, it raises the probe accuracy but barely improves interpolation quality, and its gFID is the highest of all variants. With only interpolation or only the regularization losses, the tokenizer has a higher gFID than MAETok, while InterpTok, which combines both, reaches a lower one, indicating that a generator needs both learnability and decodability. Without the alignment losses and the feature mixing ratio loss, InterpTok keeps most of its interpolation gain, but its probe accuracy falls below MAETok’s and its gFID rises far above MAETok’s, indicating that most of the learnability comes from these losses. In Table 2 , the SiT-B on MAETok’s codes nearly reaches the gFID of InterpTok’s own generator with our decoder, and the released SiT-XL improves at every number of sampling steps. Most of the generation gain thus comes from the decoder, and it comes mostly from training between codes rather than from training longer. A decoder trained just as long with only MAETok’s own losses lowers it to 10.80. When we add only our interpolation discriminator to MAETok’s losses, the gFID already drops to 9.71. To find which parts of the objective cause the gain, each row marked w/o in the lower block of Table 3 removes exactly one part from our decoder trained for 13,000 steps and keeps all the others. The six appended blocks add capacity, and removing them changes neither iFID nor gFID by more than 0.02, so the gain does not come from added capacity. In Table 21 , with the regularization losses but without interpolation, a code’s nearest neighbor belongs to its own class twice as often as with MAETok’s encoder, but the codes spread over three times as many effective dimensions. The effective dimensions are the participation ratio of the covariance spectrum, which counts the directions that carry most of the variance. With InterpTok’s encoder, the nearest neighbor belongs to its own class about as often as with this variant, while the codes spread over a third fewer effective dimensions than this variant’s. A generator models every direction along which the codes vary, and at a comparable class structure, a latent space with fewer effective dimensions is easier for a diffusion model to learn ( Zhong et al., 2026 ; Yao et al., 2025 ) . Of all these generators, only InterpTok’s combines both properties, and only its gFID falls with fewer steps.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: Diffusion generators tend to generate codes between the codes of training images, and the quality of the images decoded there predicts generation quality ( Xu et al., 2026 ) . We presented InterpTok, which trains the tokenizer there, on mixtures of the codes of two training images, with an interpolation discriminator, a mixing ratio loss and regularization losses that structure the latent space semantically. Starting from MAETok, InterpTok improves interpolation quality more than threefold, beyond every tokenizer in the comparison released by Xu et al. (2026) , and lowers the gFID by more than a quarter while keeping reconstruction quality. Its generator reaches an even lower gFID with an eighth of the sampling steps and the final gFID of MAETok’s generator after half of the training steps, and its decoder alone improves MAETok’s existing generators without retraining them. Our ablations show that a conditioned generator needs both learnability, a property of the encoder, and decodability, a property of the decoder. Training between images opens several directions for future work. App. C reports an earlier experiment in which a much smaller code trained with the interpolation objective gave more semantic interpolations. Decoders are much faster than generative models, so future work could investigate this self-supervised training objective for real-time animation, video generation or granular editing. Our findings show that the space between image codes can and should be explicitly supervised rather than ignored.

sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: This work improves image tokenizers for generation and interpolation. We train on ImageNet, and the earlier tokenizer of App. C also on ImgEdit ( Ye et al., 2025 ) , and we evaluate on ImageNet and MS-COCO under their research terms and collect no human-subject data. The images at the ends of the paths in App. C and at the corners of its squares were generated by a text-to-image model.

Generated samples of a diffusion model tend to lie between the modes of its training data ( Aithal et al., 2024 ) . The modes are the clusters of similar samples in the training data. In each sampling step, the model predicts the clean code from the noisy code as it currently looks, and the sampler moves the noisy code part of the way toward this prediction. The prediction that minimizes the denoising loss on the training data is an average of the training codes, each weighted by how well it matches the noisy code ( Xu et al., 2026 ) . When codes of several modes match, this average lies between these modes. When the noise is strong, the noisy code carries little information about the clean code, and the prediction approaches the average of all training codes ( Karras et al., 2022 ) . A conditioned generator also receives a condition, here the class label. At the strongest noise, the noisy code reveals nothing about the clean code, so the class label is the only cue, and the prediction approaches the average of the training codes of that class, which we call the class average. As the noise falls, patterns appear in the noisy code, coarse ones first and fine ones last ( Skorokhodov et al., 2025 ) , and the prediction moves away from the class average toward the average of the training codes that match these patterns. The lower the noise, the more the patterns steer the prediction. With fewer sampling steps, each step is larger, and the generator has fewer steps in which to follow the patterns that emerge in the code. It moves in larger steps toward the class average of its label and ends up closer to that average before the patterns can steer it away. Whether this helps depends on the tokenizer, since the class average is itself a code between images, the encoder decides which codes lie around it, and the decoder determines how such a code is decoded into pixel space. Stochastic and deterministic sampler. For the reported gFID values in the paper, including the results with fewer steps, Table 2 , we use the stochastic sampler with which SiT ( Ma et al., 2024 ) reports its gFID, which adds noise after each step. It is the standard choice for SiT generators and usually gives better generation results than a deterministic sampler, which adds no new noise after each step. At 250 steps, the deterministic sampler gives a worse gFID than the stochastic sampler for every generator we test, Table 16 . The reasoning in the literature for why the stochastic sampler is better is that the denoiser never predicts perfectly and every finite step adds a small step error ( Karras et al., 2022 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Xu et al., 2023 ) . Without added noise, these small errors build up more from step to step and the generation drifts further, while the added noise reduces this drift. We interpret this error as the model thinking it sees patterns in the code which it also saw during training and moving toward the average of this kind of pattern in the training samples. However, this pattern depends on the random noise and therefore might not resemble a pattern that suits the kind of image we want to generate, for example an image of a specific class. In this reading, the added noise makes the generator diverge later toward some arbitrary pattern, while with the deterministic sampler it diverges sooner. The price of adding noise is that the stochastic sampler needs more steps than a deterministic sampler, since every step also has to remove the noise added after the previous step, which makes the path less smooth ( Xu et al., 2023 ) . With the stochastic sampler, we would therefore expect every model to get worse with fewer steps. In Table 2 , every model except InterpTok does get worse, while InterpTok improves down to 32 steps. The following tests examine why InterpTok behaves differently. Fewer steps. To isolate the mechanism of the generative model, how it behaves during denoising, we use the deterministic sampler for the following tests. First, we redo the generation with different numbers of steps with the deterministic sampler, to see how the models behave with fewer steps when no noise is added, Table 16 . At 250 steps, all models, meaning MAETok, InterpTok, MAETok’s codes with our decoder and the two variants trained without interpolation and without the regularization losses, perform worse than with the stochastic sampler. MAETok’s codes with our decoder perform best, while InterpTok performs slightly worse than MAETok. However, with fewer sampling steps, the gFID of MAETok changes by less than two percent down to 16 steps and only gets worse at 8 steps, while MAETok’s codes with our decoder improve from 13.25 to 7.50 and InterpTok from 16.17 to 6.38. The two variants also improve, by about a fifth at 16 steps, but from a much worse gFID at 250 steps. So without the added noise, the gain of InterpTok from fewer steps, which we observed with the stochastic sampler, becomes even larger. We hypothesize that without added noise after each step, the deterministic sampler makes the generator pick up on patterns earlier than with the stochastic sampler, which steers the generation further away from the class condition toward similar patterns in codes it saw during training. By our hypothesis, fewer steps make each step bigger, so that the generations end closer to the class average. We estimate the class average from the codes of the 50 ImageNet validation images of each class. To test whether fewer steps bring the generated codes closer to their class average, we measure for every generated code, about 50 per class, its distance to the average code of its class, at 250, 32, 16 and 8 steps, Table 17 . With the deterministic sampler, the generated codes of all models are 15 to 18% closer to their class average at 8 steps than at 250 steps. Part of this is a general move toward the middle of the latent space, since the codes also come closer to the nearest average of another class, by 13% for MAETok and 10% for InterpTok. The distance to their own class average, however, shrinks more than the distance to the nearest other class average, more so for InterpTok, and the share of codes whose nearest class average is their own rises from 71% to 87% for InterpTok and from 38% to 48% for MAETok. With the stochastic sampler, which we measured for InterpTok and MAETok, the codes also come closer to their class average, but less so, by 13% for InterpTok and 4% for MAETok. We read this as support for the first part of our explanation, that fewer and therefore bigger steps make the generation land closer to its class average. Furthermore, we want to check the mechanism of our hypothesis, which states that early on, when the noise is strong, the class condition is the stronger cue, and that only in later steps do the patterns in the noise steer the generation more strongly. We therefore expect that in earlier steps, the generator moves the noisy code closer to its class average, and that in later steps it moves it away, so that the code is farther away from its class average and the average of another class becomes relatively closer. To check this, we measure the generator’s prediction of the finished code at each of the 250 steps for InterpTok and for MAETok, and compare its distance to the average code of its own class with its distance to the nearest class average that is not its own, Fig. 21 . Table 19 gives the values after the first and after the last step. After one step, the prediction of InterpTok is on average 2.3 times closer to the average code of its own class than to the nearest class average that is not its own. For MAETok, it is 1.5 times closer. After 250 steps, the codes of InterpTok are only 7% closer to the average code of their own class than to the nearest class average that is not their own, and the codes of MAETok are on average about as far from the average code of their own class as from the nearest class average that is not their own. Also in absolute terms, the distance of the prediction to the average code of its own class grows with every step the generator takes, as can be seen in Fig. 21 . The first step is the part that tests our hypothesis, since there the prediction of both generators lies closer to the average code of its own class than to that of any other class. That the prediction then moves away from the class average is expected, since it has to end at one particular code. We interpret this to mean that early on, when the noise is high, the generator relies more on the class condition and moves toward the average of the codes of that class, and that later it relies more on the patterns of the code, which steer it away from that average. This is our interpretation of the two generators we measured, not a claim about how diffusion models behave in general. Studies of unconditional diffusion models, which get no class label, also find that the class of an image is settled at high noise and its details at lower noise ( Biroli et al., 2024 ; Sclocchi et al., 2025 ) . If the class average comes first and the details later, this would explain why fewer steps bring the generated codes closer to their class average. With fewer and bigger steps, the generation moves further toward the early prediction, the class average, and fewer steps remain in which the later predictions can steer it away from that average. In our interpretation, with many steps, the generation follows patterns that it thinks it sees in the noise, and these can be patterns of images of any class, so the image may resemble its class less decisively. InterpTok’s decoder was trained to decode mixtures of codes, while MAETok’s decoder was never trained to handle mixtures of codes. To check whether InterpTok’s decoder therefore decodes such codes better, we average the codes of two, three, five and ten consecutive validation images of one class and decode the average with both decoders, Table 12 . We measure the Inception Score of the decoded images ( Salimans et al., 2016 ) , a standard measure that is higher the more confident an image classifier is about which class each image shows, and lower for blends of several images. As a reference, decoding the codes of single real images gives an Inception Score of about 140 with both decoders. For averages of two codes, InterpTok’s decoder still reaches 139, MAETok’s decoder only 48. For averages of three and five codes, InterpTok’s decoder reaches 131 and 92, MAETok’s decoder only 25 and 11. For averages of two such codes, the FID of the decoded images is 3.79 with InterpTok’s decoder and 35.12 with MAETok’s decoder, Table 12 . The variant trained without interpolation, whose decoder was not trained on mixtures of codes, is about as bad as MAETok, with 43.3. Finally, we check whether, with fewer steps, more of the generated images show the class they were generated for, since this is what our explanation predicts for the images and what FID rewards. The measure we use for generation quality, FID, is how well the generated images, as seen by a vision model, resemble the distribution of the dataset ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) . This is the standard metric for generation quality, and it is lower the more natural the images look and the more closely they follow the class distribution. For about 50 generated images per class, a standard ImageNet classifier, a ResNet-50, says which class each image shows, and we count how often it says the class the image was generated for, Table 22 . With the deterministic sampler, from 250 to 8 steps, this rises for InterpTok from 61% to 83% and for MAETok’s codes with our decoder from 62% to 71%, while MAETok stays at about 60%. With the stochastic sampler, the share rises for InterpTok from 68% to 71% at 32 steps and falls slightly for MAETok, from 64% to 63%. So with fewer steps, more of the images of InterpTok show the class they were made for. We read these experiments as support for our hypothesis on our generators, without claiming that they prove it or that it describes generative models in general. We show that with fewer sampling steps, where each step is bigger, the generated codes lie closer to the average code of the class used as condition for generation. We furthermore show that within 250 steps, at the start the prediction is closer to the class average and later moves away from it. Furthermore, we show that codes that lie around the class average are far more likely to be of the same class for InterpTok than for MAETok. We therefore hypothesize that the following causes the observation. With fewer steps, the generated codes are closer to the class average. Codes around the class average more often resemble that class for InterpTok. Furthermore, InterpTok was trained to decode codes that are mixtures of codes, and it decodes them into more natural images. Together, with fewer steps, the generated codes of InterpTok move toward their own class average more than toward the averages of other classes, and InterpTok’s decoder turns them into more natural images that look more like their class than with MAETok. Since FID compares the distribution of the generations with that of the dataset as viewed by a vision model, it rewards generations that adhere more closely to the class condition and have higher visual fidelity. This mechanism works less well for the two variants. For the variant trained without the regularization losses, codes near the class average were even less often of that class than with MAETok, Table 21 . The variant trained without interpolation had classes about as distinguishable as InterpTok, Table 21 , but its decoder turns mixtures of codes into images about as unnatural as MAETok’s decoder, Table 19 . Our decoder on MAETok’s codes decodes mixtures of codes about as well as InterpTok’s decoder, but MAETok’s codes around the class average are less often of that class. Without the added noise, these models still improve with fewer steps, but less than InterpTok, and with the stochastic sampler, they get worse, Table 16 .

sections.heading: D.1 Training Details of the Tokenizer
sections.text: Table 26 gives the training configuration. MAETok masks 40 to 60% of the image patches and trains three auxiliary decoders that regress histogram of oriented gradients (HOG), DINOv2-L and SigLIP-SO400M features of the masked patches from the code. A second stage freezes the encoder and fine-tunes the pixel decoder under reconstruction, perceptual and adversarial losses ( Chen et al., 2025a ) . Our fine-tune uses neither masking nor auxiliary decoders. It trains the encoder as well as the decoder, since reconstruction alone does not fix the shape of the latent space. Reshaping the latent space with an invertible map and undoing the map in the decoder leaves every reconstruction unchanged, but it changes the straight line between two codes unless the map is affine. Two tokenizers that reconstruct identically can therefore decode the line between two images differently, and the encoder decides which codes lie on this line. The CLS feature of the frozen vision model and a list of the 64 nearest neighbors are precomputed for every training image. sections.heading: D.3 Discriminator Architecture
sections.text: Backbone and heads. Both discriminators read the features of five layers of the frozen DINO ViT-S/16 backbone ( Caron et al., 2021 ) of MAETok’s discriminator, before the first block and after blocks 2, 5, 8 and 11, with the CLS token added to every patch token. Each layer carries a spectral-normalized ( Miyato et al., 2018 ) head with one logit per token, giving 5 × 196 = 980 5\times 196=980 hinge logits per image. Conditioning and passes. Each pass of the interpolation discriminator pairs the decoded mixture with one source and scores one of the two given the other. Before each of its heads, the tokens of the scored image query the keys and values of the other image at the same layer, and a k = 1 k{=}1 convolution fuses [ x ; att ; x − att ] [x;\ \mathrm{att};\ x-\mathrm{att}] , which makes their difference an explicit input. The condition thus enters through the features, as in a projection discriminator ( Miyato & Koyama, 2018 ) . With s ⁡ ( X ∣ Y ) s(X\mid Y) the per-token logit of image X X over the keys of image Y Y , the relativistic comparison of Jolicoeur-Martineau (2019) uses s real = 1 2 [ s ( A ∣ A B α ) + s ( B ∣ A B α ) ] , s fake = 1 2 [ s ( A B α ∣ A ) + s ( A B α ∣ B ) ] , ℒ D int = 1 2 𝔼 [ ( 1 − s real ) + + ( 1 + s fake ) + ] , ℒ G int = 𝔼 [ s real ] − 𝔼 [ s fake ] . \begin{gathered}s_{\mathrm{real}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\big[s(A\mid AB_{\alpha})+s(B\mid AB_{\alpha})\big],\qquad s_{\mathrm{fake}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\big[s(AB_{\alpha}\mid A)+s(AB_{\alpha}\mid B)\big],\\ \mathcal{L}_{D}^{\mathrm{int}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}\big[(1-s_{\mathrm{real}})_{+}+(1+s_{\mathrm{fake}})_{+}\big],\qquad\mathcal{L}_{G}^{\mathrm{int}}=\mathbb{E}[s_{\mathrm{real}}]-\mathbb{E}[s_{\mathrm{fake}}].\end{gathered} (7) Each mixture is thus scored four times, and the two real and the two fake passes are averaged before the hinge. The reconstruction discriminator is an unconditional head that compares real images with their reconstructions, since a head conditioned on the source would classify any departure from it as fake, and conditioning is known to cause mode collapse in generative adversarial networks ( Goodfellow et al., 2014 ) trained on limited data ( Shahbazi et al., 2022 ) . It is separate from the interpolation discriminator, since mixtures are easier to detect as fake than reconstructions and could dominate a shared head. sections.heading: D.4 Decoder Architecture
sections.text: MAETok’s decoder has 12 ViT blocks of width 768 over 256 image tokens. Each of the six appended blocks computes x + g ⁡ ( block ⁡ ( x ) − x ) x+g\,(\mathrm{block}(x)-x) with a scalar gate g g initialized at zero, and its rotary frequencies are copied from the pretrained decoder. The appended blocks add 43.1M parameters to the 173.9M of the released checkpoint.

sections.heading: D.5 Pair Sampling
sections.text: In each epoch, every training image is paired with its most similar unpaired image among its k k nearest neighbors, measured by the cosine similarity of the CLS features of the frozen vision model. We pair similar images because, by the analysis of Xu et al. (2026) , at low noise the samples of a diffusion model gather near the straight line between two neighboring training codes. Yue et al. (2026) train the neighborhood of one code, while we train the whole line between two codes. The number k k grows from 8 to 128 over the epochs, Table 26 , so the pairs become less similar as training proceeds. Only the 64 nearest neighbors are precomputed, and for k > 64 k>64 an image takes such a neighbor with probability 64 / k 64/k and a random unpaired image otherwise. Each micro-batch holds four pairs, eight images, and mixes all 28 pairs of its images. Four of these mixtures therefore combine two paired, similar images, and the other 24 combine images from different pairs.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.16759v1 [cs.CV] 12 Oct 2026 Image Tokenizers Should Be Trained Between Images Ole Beißwenger Jan-Niklas Dihlmann & Hendrik Lensch Affiliation: University of Tübingen Abstract Latent diffusion models generate images as codes of an image tokenizer, whose decoder turns them into the pixel image. Recent tokenizers improve how well these codes reconstruct an image and how easily a generator learns them. Yet a generator does not reproduce the codes of training images, and when a generated code lands outside what the decoder expects, the decoded image contains imperfections. Current methods make the decoder more robust to generated codes by adding noise during training. However, generated codes lie between the training codes and resemble their mixture more than one of them plus noise. To improve generated images, decoders should therefore be trained on codes in the space between training samples. We propose InterpTok , which fine-tunes MAETok to decode mixtures of image codes into natural images. Since no target image exists between two training samples, a discriminator judges whether each decoded mixture looks as natural as its two sources. A mixing ratio loss requires the decoded mixture to keep the mixing ratio of the two codes. Together, they prevent collapse to a trivial solution and yield a sharp and natural composition of both images. InterpTok keeps MAETok’s reconstruction quality and improves interpolation quality more than threefold, the best of all tokenizers in a recent benchmark. Beyond interpolation, InterpTok improves the generation FID of a matched diffusion transformer from 11.61 to 8.48 without guidance, and even reaches 8.11 at an eighth of the sampling steps, where the generator on MAETok’s codes worsens. The generator trained on our tokenizer also reaches the final result of the one trained on MAETok at half the training steps. Our findings show that the space between image codes can and should be explicitly supervised rather than ignored. Figure 1: Overview. Reconstruction trains the tokenizer at the codes of images A and B, never on the line between them. InterpTok trains it there, and the codes on the line between them decode to natural images that change from A toward B, where MAETok superimposes the two images. 1 Introduction Modern image generation largely relies on diffusion and flow matching models ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Ma et al., 2024 ) . These models generate images through many refinement steps, so most operate in a compact latent space to make each step more efficient ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) . In this space, each image is represented by a compact code created by an image tokenizer. The tokenizer’s encoder turns images into codes, and its decoder turns codes back into images. The generator learns to produce these codes and therefore depends on the space created by the tokenizer. Improving image generation therefore starts with asking what makes this latent space useful for a generator. Most tokenizer methods focus on the codes of the training images and make them easier for a generator to learn ( Chen et al., 2025a ; Yao et al., 2025 ; Fan et al., 2026 ) . Standard tokenizer training, however, supervises one code at a time by reconstructing its image. It tells the decoder what to produce at the codes of the training images, but does not supervise the codes between them. As Fig. 1 illustrates, a decoder can reconstruct images A and B well and still turn a mixture of their codes into a blurry superposition. Reconstruction can therefore give us good endpoints while leaving the path between them undefined. This gap matters because a generator does not perfectly reproduce training samples but creates codes the decoder never saw. Recent work shows that generated codes lie near the lines between neighboring training codes. It also shows that the quality of images decoded on these lines predicts generation quality better than reconstruction quality does ( Xu et al., 2026 ) . The decoder must therefore work beyond the exact codes it was trained to reconstruct. Existing tokenizer and decoder training schemes add noise to training codes and make their local neighborhoods more robust ( Yang et al., 2026b ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) . They improve the visual quality of images decoded around each image code. While this improves generation, it does not target the space between training codes, where generative denoising models tend to place their codes. In this work, we argue that image tokenizers should be trained between images. We propose InterpTok, which mixes the codes of two training images at a known ratio and decodes the result. Each pair gives us an entire line of training inputs, even though no target image exists along that line. To prevent trivial solutions such as copying one source, we set two requirements the decoded mixtures must fulfill. The decoded mixture must look like a natural image, and it must remain tied to its position between the two sources. Our first component, the interpolation objective , addresses both. An interpolation discriminator compares the decoded mixture with one source at a time in the features of a frozen pretrained network and pushes it away from blurry overlays ( Caron et al., 2021 ; Sauer et al., 2021 ) . A mixing ratio loss prevents the decoder from choosing either source and keeps the result at the mixing ratio, in pixels and in the features of a frozen vision model ( Siméoni et al., 2026 ) . Together, they enforce natural-looking images that are true compositions of both sources at the right ratio, allowing supervision without target images. Interpolation and reconstruction alone do not guarantee a latent space that a generator can learn easily. In our ablations, the interpolation objective improves the visual fidelity and sharpness of images between codes, but leaving out losses that structure the latent space makes the codes harder for the generator to learn. We therefore introduce a second component, regularization losses . They align the codes with the features of the same vision model, so that images with similar content receive similar codes ( Yao et al., 2025 ) . MAETok structures its codes too, through auxiliary decoders that predict pretrained features of masked image parts, and our regularization losses replace them. InterpTok combines the interpolation objective and the regularization losses with the original reconstruction objective of MAETok ( Chen et al., 2025a ) . Our contributions can be summarized as follows: • Training Between Images: We propose a training principle for latent image tokenizers that supervises the space between image codes. An interpolation discriminator and a mixing ratio loss make the decoded mixture of two codes a natural image at the right ratio. • InterpTok: Trained end to end with the interpolation objective and our regularization losses, InterpTok improves interpolation quality more than threefold and generation quality by more than a quarter and lets its generator train and sample faster, while keeping the reconstruction quality of MAETok. • Fast Decoder Fine-Tuning: For MAETok, whose latent space is already structured, fine-tuning only the decoder with our objective is a cheap way to improve the generators already trained on it, without retraining them. 2 Related Work Image tokenizers. The objective of image tokenizers is to compress images into a compact latent space and to decode the codes back to images. A generative model can then be trained in this compressed space, improving efficiency and performance ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) . Early tokenizers were plain autoencoders trained to reconstruct their input ( Hinton & Salakhutdinov, 2006 ) , which leaves the shape of their latent space unconstrained. Variational autoencoders add a penalty that keeps the code distribution close to a Gaussian, which makes the latent space easier for a generator to learn ( Kingma & Welling, 2014 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ) . Compression loses information, so the optimum of a pure pixel loss is an average of the possible images, which blurs the reconstructions. VQ-GAN therefore adds a discriminator that judges whether reconstructed images look natural ( Esser et al., 2021 ) . All of them train the decoder on the codes of single images, and none trains it between two images. More recent work shapes the latent space itself instead of optimizing reconstruction alone, with 1D codes whose tokens are not tied to patches in the image ( Yu et al., 2024 ) and with codes aligned to the features of pretrained vision models ( Yao et al., 2025 ) . MAETok ( Chen et al., 2025a ) showed that a diffusion model learns the codes more easily when they form fewer and more separated clusters, and reached this structure with a plain autoencoder trained by masked modeling, where auxiliary decoders predict features of the hidden image patches from the codes. Because masking degrades reconstruction, MAETok then freezes the encoder and fine-tunes only the pixel decoder for a few epochs, which improves fine detail. Behavior of generative denoising models. Generative denoising models do not simply recreate the image codes they saw during training. This can lead to generated codes that deviate from the codes the decoder was optimized for. These out-of-distribution codes are then decoded to images with blur or artifacts. Recent work therefore trains the decoder on codes other than the clean training codes, by transforming the code ( Kouzelis et al., 2025 ) , mixing it with noise ( Yang et al., 2026b ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) or post-training on the samples of a trained generator ( Qiu et al., 2025 ) . However, Aithal et al. (2024) showed that a diffusion model interpolates between nearby modes of its training data and produces samples that exist nowhere in it, which they call mode interpolation. Xu et al. (2026) carried this to tokenizer codes, where the optimal denoiser outputs a weighted average of the training codes ( Karras et al., 2022 ) . They show empirically that the quality of decoded mixtures of image codes (iFID) predicts the generation quality (gFID) far better than reconstruction quality (rFID), which is uncorrelated with it or even negatively correlated. Generated codes therefore resemble mixtures of image codes. Supervising between images. Training an autoencoder on interpolation goes back to representation learning, where a realistic interpolation was taken as a sign that the autoencoder had captured the structure of its data instead of memorizing it ( Berthelot et al., 2019 ) . ACAI trains the autoencoder so that its decoded mixtures fool a critic that regresses the mixing coefficient ( Berthelot et al., 2019 ) , AMR ( Beckham et al., 2019 ) and Oring et al. (2021) train it against a discriminator between real and mixed images, and GAIA against an autoencoder that is trained to reconstruct real images but not mixtures ( Sainburg et al., 2018 ) . ACAI and AMR report smoother interpolations of small images, and codes that are more useful for classification. Recently, CompTok ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) argued that a generator learns a token space more easily when the images decoded along the line between the codes of two nearby images stay realistic, and measured this as mode connectivity. To raise it, CompTok trains on codes formed by swapping token subsets between two images under an adversarial realism term, but a swap composes real token values, whereas a generator produces values between two real ones ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , and CompTok does not train on the line it measures. The gap between swapped and generated values arises only for continuous tokens, as in MAETok and CompTok, since a generator of discrete tokens only selects real codebook entries. InterpTok is an image tokenizer trained to decode mixtures of image codes into sharp, natural images that combine both sources. It adds two components to the reconstruction objective of MAETok. The interpolation objective trains the decoder on mixtures of the codes of two images with an interpolation discriminator, which judges each decoded mixture beside one of its two source images, and two mixing ratio losses, which require the decoded mixture to be a composition at the ratio at which the two codes were mixed. The regularization losses structure the latent space semantically. Fig. 2 gives an overview. 3.1 Background Latent diffusion. Latent diffusion models generate images in the compact latent space of an image tokenizer instead of in pixel space, since training generative models on pixels is computationally expensive ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) . The tokenizer consists of an encoder E E and a decoder D D . The encoder maps an image A A to its code a = E ⁡ ( A ) a=E(A) , which is much smaller than the image itself. The decoder maps a code back to an image. Both are trained together, so that the decoded image D ⁡ ( E ⁡ ( A ) ) D(E(A)) is close to the original image A A . A diffusion generator is then trained separately to denoise noisy image codes. To generate an image, the generator starts from pure noise and iteratively refines it into a code, which D D then decodes into the pixel image ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Ma et al., 2024 ) . Diffusion generators tend to generate codes that lie between the codes of training images ( Aithal et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . The decoder of the tokenizer, however, is trained only on the codes that the encoder produces for training images, leaving the codes between them unsupervised. MAETok. We build on MAETok ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , which shows that a diffusion model learns codes more easily when a Gaussian mixture model fits them with fewer modes. MAETok obtains such codes with a plain autoencoder, without the penalty of a variational autoencoder. Its code consists of 128 vectors, called tokens. MAETok is trained in two stages. In the first stage, a large part of every image is masked before it enters the encoder. Small auxiliary decoders then predict, from the code, the features that pretrained vision models extract from the masked parts, extending masked autoencoders ( He et al., 2022 ) from pixels to features. Masking forces the encoder to infer the hidden parts of an image from the visible ones, which leads to such codes. However, a decoder trained on the codes of partly masked images reconstructs fewer details. To address this, the second stage freezes the encoder and fine-tunes only the decoder on the codes of complete images, which recovers the lost details. We choose MAETok for three reasons. First, we want to show that our method is not limited to the decoder, and therefore choose among tokenizers that train their own encoder. Among those in the benchmark of Xu et al. (2026) that do not start from a pretrained vision model, MAETok has the highest interpolation quality. We attribute this to its masked training, where the decoder is trained to reconstruct the complete image from the code of a partly masked image. Second, its codes are continuous. In a quantized tokenizer, every token is an index into a codebook, and there is no code between two indices. Third, MAETok is a 1D tokenizer ( Yu et al., 2024 ) , whose tokens are not tied to locations in the image, while every token of a 2D tokenizer belongs to one patch. We want mixtures that interpolate between whole images, not between the patches at each location. Reconstruction objective. MAETok trains with the standard tokenizer losses ( Esser et al., 2021 ) , a pixel loss, a perceptual loss ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) and an adversarial loss. The pixel loss and the perceptual loss compare the decoded image with the original image, in pixels and in the features of a pretrained network. The adversarial loss trains the tokenizer against a discriminator that distinguishes real images from reconstructions. It enforces sharp images, whereas the optimum of a pure pixel loss is a slightly blurred image. Unlike the other two losses, it needs no target image, since the discriminator judges each image on its own. We denote these losses together as the reconstruction objective ℒ rec \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}} and their discriminator as the reconstruction discriminator. 3.2 The Space Between Two Codes We study the codes between the codes of two training images. Recent methods add noise to the codes during decoder training ( Yang et al., 2026b ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) , which makes the decoder more robust around each training code but does not target the space between codes. A straightforward alternative is to supervise random codes, so that every code decodes to a realistic image. However, since real images have few intrinsic dimensions ( Pope et al., 2021 ) , their codes occupy only a small part of the latent space, and random codes mostly lie far outside the training distribution. Decoding a meaningful image from an arbitrary code is far more ambiguous than decoding one between two image codes. A mixture has no target image either, but it comes with two sources and a ratio, and InterpTok uses them in place of a target image. Decodability and learnability. Two properties of a tokenizer matter for the quality of the output of a diffusion generator. We call the visual fidelity and sharpness of the images that the decoder produces from generated codes its decodability. We call how easily a conditioned generator can learn the codes of training images and tell them apart by their condition, such as their class label, the learnability of the tokenizer. This is easier when the latent space is structured such that the class of an image can be derived from where its code lies, as MAETok finds. Decodability is thus mainly a property of the decoder, and learnability of the encoder. InterpTok targets decodability with the interpolation objective of Sec. 3.3 and learnability with the regularization losses of Sec. 3.4 . 3.3 Interpolation Objective The interpolation objective trains the tokenizer on decoded mixtures and targets decodability. It consists of an interpolation discriminator and two mixing ratio losses. Interpolation discriminator. A mixture has no target image, and we therefore supervise the decoded mixture with a discriminator. Adversarial interpolation was introduced for representation learning with small autoencoders. ACAI ( Berthelot et al., 2019 ) trains a critic to recover the mixing ratio from the decoded mixture and the autoencoder to hide it, and AMR ( Beckham et al., 2019 ) trains a discriminator that tells real images from decoded mixtures, both on small images such as MNIST, SVHN and CIFAR-10. Their critics judge the mixture alone, so any realistic image passes, whether or not it relates to the two sources, and neither keeps the mixture at the mixing ratio. Our interpolation discriminator judges the decoded mixture beside one of its sources and is trained to identify which of the two is the real image. We use it to train a tokenizer for latent diffusion on ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) at 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution. For an image X X and a second image Y Y , the features of X X in a frozen DINO network ( Caron et al., 2021 ) attend to those of Y Y through trained cross-attention layers, so that every part of X X is compared with Y Y . We therefore add regularization losses to structure the latent space semantically. The frozen DINOv3 model, pretrained on large image collections, describes each image by a feature vector. Alignment losses make the codes carry the semantic information of these features. VA-VAE ( Yao et al., 2025 ) aligns the code of a tokenizer with the patch features of such a model, DINOv2 ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) , at every image position and requires the similarities between the positions of a code to match those between the features. REPA ( Yu et al., 2025 ) requires the features to be predictable by a small network from the hidden states of a diffusion generator, and GigaTok ( Xiong et al., 2025 ) from the activations inside the decoder of a tokenizer. InterpTok uses three alignment losses in this spirit, which require the similarities between the codes of different images to match those between their feature vectors, the feature vector to be predictable from the code, and the features of each image patch to be predictable from the activations inside the decoder. As a result, images with more similar visual and semantic features receive more similar codes, which these works find easier for a generator to learn. MAETok ties its codes to pretrained features as well, through auxiliary decoders that predict the features of the masked image parts, and InterpTok replaces these auxiliary decoders with the three alignment losses. The representation Fréchet loss ( Yang et al., 2026a ) was introduced for post-training generators, and to our knowledge it has not been used to train a tokenizer before. It compares the distribution of the decoded images with that of the training images in the features of three frozen image encoders, SigLIP2 ( Tschannen et al., 2025 ) , Inception-v3 ( Szegedy et al., 2016 ) and MAE ( He et al., 2022 ) , and minimizes the Fréchet distance between the two. (2026) , and ablate its components. Our experiments validate three claims. First, a modern tokenizer can be trained between images together with current regularization losses.
